comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed about this graph is that red completely dominates the entire country. But, in my town, and on the east coast of Massachusetts in general, Hilary Clinton had the majority of the votes. In my precinct in particular, she had 52% of the votes, while Trump only had 39% of the votes. Massachusetts appears to be the state with the highest percentage of Hilary supporters, and New England in general seems to be the region that supports Hilary the most. But, while all counties in Massachusetts voted the majority for Hilary Clinton, there are some towns that voted for Trump. In fact, in one of the towns adjacent to my own, Donald Trump received 52% of the votes. This leads me to wonder how two towns that are so close and so similar can have completely different outcomes in their election results. I also wondered how the election was so close considering most of the map was red. The answer to that question, I realized, was that many of the most densely populated cities in the country voted for Hilary, while many sparsely populated areas voted for Trump. If I were to come up with a title for this graph, it would be “Why the Colors May Not Tell the Whole Story,” because this graph does not appear to be an accurate representation of how close the election was.

comments.raw_comment: Where I live, Hampstead, New Hampshire, voting follows the national trend in supporting Trump. In my town, 58% of voters or 3,186 people voted for Donald Trump while 36% of voters or 1,996 people voted for Hilary Clinton. In Lawrence, Massachusetts, where a large population of Hispanic and Black voters lives, Hilary is favored to 86% over Trump’s 10%. My question is this: should we consider the electoral college outdated? Wouldn’t it make sense for majority votes to dictate the outcome of elections? This map is meant to physically illustrate how the country tended to vote during the 2016 Presidential Election. The discoloration on the graph is there to indicate which states, regions, and towns voted for which primary candidate, and how popular the candidate is in the recorded data.   If I was to create a title for the map shown, “America Is More Purple Than We Are Led to Believe” seems to be the most fitting. Since popular vote was in favor of Clinton (by a small margin), but the electoral college votes tilted towards Trump, America is in a time of political separation; there are seemingly equal amounts of people that support each candidate in each party, it’s just that distribution of the votes that create a majority “red” map.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed when I first looked at the map was that it appears that the red areas, which are areas that voted Republican, seem to dominate the map of the country. Then my eye started to gravitate towards the Massachusetts area and I noticed that it was blue, and the states directly North and South of Massachusetts seem to create this blue line down the Eastern coast of the country that stops and curves above Florida and continues West until Alabama. I began looking for other blue areas and I noticed that the West coast (California and Washington) seems to follow a similar trend, skipping over Oregon. I then searched for how my town and the surrounding towns voted and found that they mostly voted for Clinton, with my town divided 63% for Clinton and 27% for Trump. The map showed me that the closest Trump area to my town was Peabody, about a 17-minute drive away. It was interesting to see how my town voted compared to the state and to the entire country. Something that I wondered was how the election results were so close when the map seems to depict such a large gap between Trump voters and Clinton voters. If I were to write a headline for this map, it would be “The Importance of Zooming in on the Bigger Picture” because the story this map is telling is that Trump swept the country, however in reality we know that the win was actually quite narrow.

For example, it was a landslide for Clinton in Lawrence, but in Pelham, NH Trump won by a majority.  Other suburban towns, like my hometown, Andover,  voted for Clinton, but not as strongly.   I cannot help but wonder why these  communities voted so differently given their geographic proximity.   Is it related to average income, presence of children, average age, ethnic background?  The map coloring does not tell the full story.  Also, I'm curious how this map changed during the course of the election related to polling.  Was it accurate?  And how did the Democratic/Republic vote in this election compare with last presidential election.  Did people vote candidates or party?  This map does not give a good representation and the color coding is misleading to what happened during the election because we know it was roughly equal during the time of the election
